claim: Aggregate benchmark gains from a skill edit imply no item-level regressions

evidence.quote: admits permanent regressions, since an edit can raise the average while breaking items the skill already solves
exposes regressions that an aggregate score hides
13 of 87 tasks show negative Skills deltas
significant negative flips (up to more than 60%) exist for a variety of base model update scenarios and downstream tasks.

note: SAGE measured 2.4-45.6% of already-solved validation items broken by edits accepted under a naive aggregate gate (Table 1 values, not quotes). SkillsBench and SWE-Skills-Bench show averages above harmful tasks and skills. The CONTRADICTIONS.md wording 'aggregate improvement does not show item-level regressions are absent' is a paraphrase, not a verbatim 2609.36043 quote.

claim: Cross-harness benchmark charts support model admission decisions

evidence.quote: Because Terminal-Bench is an interactive framework, agent and model performance are hard to decouple.
The agent scaffold used to report each model was chosen to maximize performance.
The choice of scaffold has the single biggest impact on the overall performance.
simply switching the scaffold makes up to an 11% difference for GPT-5

note: Fixed-model harness swaps move scores by about 6-17 pp, and the direction is unstable (vendor harness wins in SkillsBench, Terminus 2 beats Claude Code for Opus 4.5 on Terminal-Bench). Terminal-Bench still concludes model selection usually matters more than scaffold, so charts are not useless, but they are not controlled comparisons. Epoch's post states the authors' views.

claim: Published studies report item-level regressions alongside gains for prompt or skill optimization

evidence.quote: the fraction of the items the current skill already solves that an accepted edit breaks
13 of 87 tasks show negative Skills deltas
92 of 98 skills have no statistically significant effect
from a pass ratio of 83.20 to 66.24

note: Confirmed, with limits. SAGE (skill optimization) reports per-item regression rates, but in-sample and without seeds. SkillsBench and SWE-Skills-Bench report per-task or per-skill harm, but compare skill vs no skill rather than an edit. Mainstream prompt-optimizer papers (GEPA, MIPROv2, ACE) report aggregates only.

claim: Naive aggregate-gated skill edits break a large share of already-solved items, and a paired exact gate removes most of it

evidence.quote: a per-item paired comparison that evaluates the current skill and the edited skill on identical validation items, which exposes regressions that an aggregate score hides and penalizes them asymmetrically
filtering out those whose gains are unreliable or purchased by breaking already-solved items
the validation set is reused across optimization steps, so trajectory-level error rates are not controlled

note: Table 1 values (not quotes): naive gate 2.4-45.6% regression rate across 5 benchmarks x 4 backbones; SAGE lower in 19 of 20 settings, mostly 0.0%, highest final score in 20 of 20 (+8.73 average). One optimizer (SkillOpt), in-sample validation items, seeds not reported. The gate is a one-sided exact binomial test that equals exact McNemar at lambda = 1.

claim: Curated skills raise average pass rate while some tasks regress

evidence.quote: from 33.9% to 50.5% (+16.6 percentage points...)
13 of 87 tasks show negative Skills deltas
The common cause is a single 'correct' pipeline without applicability boundaries or lightweight fallbacks.

note: Same pinned container and model per configuration, three trials per cell, paired deltas, 95% CIs in figures (Appendix G not read). Largest task drops are -7.4 pp, which at three trials per cell is one or two flipped trials, so individual task regressions are not established. v1 reported 16 of 84 negative tasks and +16.2 pp.

claim: Self-generated skills improve agents over a no-skills baseline

evidence.quote: land below the no-Skills baseline on all three configurations

note: Current SkillsBench: -8.1 pp (Claude Code + Opus 4.7), -11.3 pp (Codex + GPT-5.5), -11.5 pp (Gemini CLI + Gemini 3.1 Pro), against +18.2 to +24.8 pp for curated skills on the same configurations. Earlier versions are cited elsewhere as +0.0 pp (Library Drift abstract) or -1.3 pp (secondhand), so the magnitude is version-dependent; none shows a benefit.

claim: Repository context files (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md) generally improve coding-agent task success

evidence.quote: does not generally improve task success rates
LLM-generated context files have a marginal negative effect on task success rates
all context files consistently increase the cost and number of steps required to complete tasks
We sample completions for each agent once.

note: Harness and model held fixed, context file varied. None vs LLM-generated CMH p = 0.87 and 0.37; None vs developer-written +2.4 pp, p = 0.21; cost increase significant. Single runs and aggregates only, with no per-task gain/regression table. Lulla et al. (2601.20404, snippet only) report efficiency gains but do not test correctness.

claim: Most public agent skills have no measurable effect, and a few cause large regressions

evidence.quote: 92 of 98 skills have no statistically significant effect
from a pass ratio of 83.20 to 66.24
an exact two-sided paired sign-flip test

note: asyncio-patterns is -16.96 pp and negative in all four configurations. github-actions-templates is -5.14 overall but -22.78 pp under Claude Code + Haiku 4.5 (outputs written to .github/workflows/ instead of ci/). One run with and one without per requirement per configuration, so 'no significant effect' has limited power.

claim: arXiv 2606.16523 (SkillWiki) measures agent task outcomes of governed skill edits

evidence.quote: 99 were successfully converted into governed skill candidates
the effectiveness of the proposed infrastructure and governance workflow,
the downstream impact of SkillWiki on diverse agent benchmarks.

note: The second and third quotes come from the Limitations section: the evaluation measures the former and not the latter. The rest of the evaluation is a single-artifact lifecycle case study (S0-S7), and Appendix B defines success and failure rate formulas without reporting values. The critique in CONTRADICTIONS.md is accurate.

claim: For a fixed model, harness choice moves agent benchmark scores more than typical context-file or skill effects

evidence.quote: Gemini-2.5-Pro sees a 17% increase in resolution rate when paired with Terminus 2 instead of OpenHands
simply switching the scaffold makes up to an 11% difference for GPT-5
up to a 15% difference for Kimi K2 Thinking

note: Opus 4.5 scores 57.8 / 52.1 / 51.9% on Terminus 2 / Claude Code / OpenHands (Terminal-Bench Table 2). SkillsBench has Opus 4.7 at 61.2% (Claude Code) vs 53.1% (OpenHands). Gloaguen's context-file deltas are at most 8 pp and not significant. The 2606.20683 harness-survey 13.7 pp figure is secondhand and not used.

claim: Single-run agent evaluations can distinguish a 2-3 pp skill or prompt effect from noise

evidence.quote: single-run pass@1 estimates vary by 2.2 to 6.0 percentage points depending on which run is selected
with standard deviations exceeding 1.5 percentage points even at temperature 0
reported improvements of 2–3 percentage points may reflect evaluation noise rather than genuine algorithmic progress.
Detecting a 2% improvement at p<0.05 with 80% power requires approximately 9 runs per agent under test.

note: Ten runs of six configurations on SWE-bench Verified. A 1-point effect needs about 36 runs at median variance. Gloaguen and SWE-Skills-Bench use one run per condition; SkillsBench uses 3 trials, Terminal-Bench at least 5. The paper does not publish the share of flaky instances.

claim: Model updates that raise aggregate accuracy still flip previously correct items to wrong

evidence.quote: negative flips -- previously correct instances are now predicted incorrectly.
We find more negative flips for model updates with a smaller delta in performance gain.
significant negative flips (up to more than 60%) exist for a variety of base model update scenarios and downstream tasks.

note: MUSCLE binary-task NFR is about 3-12% (e.g. GSM8K Llama 1->2 8.49%, HellaSwag Vicuna 10.48%; table values). The 'up to more than 60%' figure includes smooth NFR on generative tasks, which counts any per-item score decrease. Ma et al. (2311.11123) figures (10.9% correct->wrong; 87.9% of accuracy-improving updates regressed at least one item) are paraphrased in the fetch summary and not quoted here. Xie et al.'s QQP 8x figure is secondhand.

claim: Adding instructions to a prompt degrades joint compliance even when per-instruction compliance stays high

evidence.quote: 68% accuracy at the max density of 500 instructions
bias towards earlier instructions

note: ManyIFEval/StyleMBPP values (2509.21051, table values, not quotes): Claude 3.5 Sonnet StyleMBPP prompt-level 0.96 -> 0.01 from 1 to 6 instructions while instruction-level stays 0.80; GPT-4o ManyIFEval prompt-level 0.94 -> 0.21 at 10. IFScale is abstract-only. Stable code correctness under style instructions is secondhand.

claim: Prompt optimizers such as MIPROv2 and GEPA never regress below baseline at benchmark level

evidence.quote: lead to performance degradation when used with Qwen3 8B.
For each training instance, GEPA records the highest score across all candidates, forming a Pareto frontier.

note: GEPA Table 1 on Qwen3 8B (values, not quotes): MIPROv2 IFBench 36.22 vs 36.90 baseline, AIME-2025 20.00 vs 27.33, LiveBench-Math 46.60 vs 48.70; GEPA+Merge IFBench 28.23. Plain GEPA has no benchmark below baseline. Per-instance scores are used inside the optimizer, not reported; no seeds, CIs or significance tests in the text read (first ~100k characters). ACE likewise reports split aggregates without seeds.

claim: Rewriting accumulated agent context can fall below the no-adaptation baseline

evidence.quote: at step 60 the context contained 18,282 tokens and achieved an accuracy of 66.7
at the very next step it collapsed to just 122 tokens, with accuracy dropping to 57.1
the baseline accuracy of 63.7 without adaptation

note: ACE calls this context collapse and also names brevity bias. One reported event, no seeds. Library Drift (2605.19576, abstract-only) reports a related silent failure in self-evolving skill libraries.

claim: Regression-gated skill acceptance is shown to transfer out of distribution

evidence.quote: lifts each of them in-domain and none of them out of distribution
overfit the validation set and do not transfer

note: GRASP is abstract-only; its regression-budget values and per-task regressions were not read. The SAGE quote describes lucky edits under the naive gate (Optimizer's Curse). SAGE does not report held-out-test regression rates. 2605.26655 (abstract-only) reports that optimized prompts often fail to transfer across benchmarks.

claim: A published study combines same harness and model, repeated runs or seeds, a held-out set and per-item flip reporting for an edit to a prompt, skill or context file

evidence.quote: No study found combines same harness, same model, multiple independent optimization seeds, held-out test sets, and per-item flip reporting.
I found no study that runs the same harness and model with a skill or context-file edit (v1 vs v2 of the same file) and reports per-task flips with repeated runs.

note: None found, not proven absent. SAGE has paired per-item regression on an optimizer trajectory but no seeds and in-sample validation. SkillsBench has repeats and pairing but fixed skill sets and no flip counts. SWE-Skills-Bench uses a paired test with single runs. Gloaguen uses single runs and aggregates. Designer RSI (matched replay gate) and RepairGate are secondhand and unread. MIPROv2, TextGrad, EvoPrompt and PromptBreeder primary texts were not checked.
